conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Dr. Maya Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I work with new moms to make sure emotional ups and downs don’t get overlooked in all the baby-care hustle.  

Today I’ll be giving you the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up any time in the first year after birth. There’s also a question about self-harm, because safety is always priority one.  

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me you’re in danger; then we’ll make a plan together to keep you safe. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you in the past seven days. Ready when you are.

To start: in the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt pretty impossible?

I’ve still been able to laugh sometimes—like when my sister sent me that silly video—but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. Mostly I have to remind myself to join in when everyone else is laughing; the joy feels kind of muted.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, that’s about right—sometimes I can laugh, but it doesn’t feel as natural or bright as it did before the baby.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like taking the baby for walks or having my morning coffee—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. It feels more like going through the motions than real enjoyment.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. When the baby wouldn’t settle at 2 a.m. I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right or I missed his sleepy cues. I know, rationally, that babies just cry, but the thought still jumps in that it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I do get those waves of worry, even when everything seems fine. Like, I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing in the other room, or if that tiny rash is something serious. I can usually talk myself down pretty quickly, but it keeps popping up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes my heart just starts racing—like when I’m walking to the mailbox—but I’m not sure why. It passes in a minute or two, and I can calm myself by taking slow breaths, so it hasn’t stopped me from doing things. Still, it’s unsettling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I can keep everything afloat, but yes—there’ve been moments this week where it feels like the dishes, the laundry, the feedings, the texts I haven’t answered are all piling up and I’m one step behind. I handle it, but it leaves me kind of drained and flustered.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I do feel a little down sometimes, but I’ve still been able to sleep pretty well. Once I finally drop off, I stay asleep—unless the baby wakes me—though it can take me a bit longer to nod off if I’m churning through the to-do list in my head.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah, I’ve had stretches where I just feel kind of heavy and teary, especially in the evenings. It’s not all day, but most days there’s at least a little window where I feel pretty low.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I’ve cried a couple of times this week—mostly when everything feels piled up or when the baby won’t settle and I’m running on fumes. It’s not constant, but the tears come easier than they used to.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and overwhelmed, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

You've shared that, over the past week, laughter and excitement feel muted, worry bubbles up out of nowhere, and you've had moments of feeling overwhelmed, self-critical, and tearful. These emotional shifts are understandably concerning for a new mom, and they deserve attention and support.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment compared to before, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses self-blame "a few times this week," fitting "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes repeated, intrusive worries despite reassurance, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden racing heart with no clear trigger, occurring "sometimes" and causing distress, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports repeated moments of feeling overwhelmed and drained, consistent with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Response indicates frequent but not constant sadness, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 15 on the EPDS falls within the ≥14 range, indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med> and warrants urgent referral. The patient describes <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>daily tearfulness</sym>, <sym>increased self-reproach</sym>, and recurrent <sym>anxiety</sym> with <sym>panic-like sensations</sym>, meeting DSM-5 threshold criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> (≥5 symptoms, same 2-week period, causing clinically significant distress). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent follow-up with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next week
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health therapist</med> for cognitive-behavioural or interpersonal therapy
3. Discuss possible benefits and safety of <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
4. Share results with a trusted partner or family member so they can help monitor mood and support appointments
5. Schedule a brief re-screen (EPDS) in 2 weeks to track symptom trajectory
6. Continue gentle daily walks and 10-15 min personal downtime; both modestly lift mood and reduce <sym>anxiety</sym>
7. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or progressive muscle relaxation when <sym>heart racing</sym> or <sym>worry spikes</sym> occur
8. Keep a simple log of mood, crying spells, and sleep; bring it to your provider visit
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 2 wks post-delivery

Patient-reported symptoms  
- Diminished enjoyment/pleasure in previously rewarding activities (Q2)  
- Daily low mood, “heavy and teary” most evenings; crying 2× this week (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Frequent, unprovoked worries about infant safety; brief heart-racing episodes with spontaneous resolution (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks; reports “drained and flustered” (Q6)  
- Sleep onset delay related to mental “to-do list,” but no sustained insomnia (Q7)  

Observed patterns  
- Mild-to-moderate anhedonia and labile tearfulness consistent with depressive spectrum  
- Prominent generalized/perinatal anxiety without functional avoidance  
- No self-harm ideation, intent, or plan (Q10) – safety screen negative  

Screening significance  
Meets partial criteria for postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; severity appears sub-threshold but clinically meaningful. Close monitoring or formal assessment (e.g., EPDS, PHQ-9, GAD-7) recommended within 1–2 weeks.
